summary: Two baselines evaluating: (A) dual-track extraction value, (B) multilingual literature coverage value

baseline_a.title: Dual-Track Extraction Value
baseline_a.question: Does extracting evidence from both original-language and translated tracks yield better results than either track alone?
baseline_a.dataset: Fused-75 dev set (10 entries with source-visible adjudication)
baseline_a.methodology: Same preprocessed Phase 2 extraction artifacts evaluated under three track configurations against the same ground truth

unique_contributions.interpretation: Translated track contributes 5 unique fields (segregation + functional evidence) that the original track misses. Original track contributes variant typing. Dual-track combines both.

baseline_a.conclusion: Dual-track extraction improves F1 by +5.5% over English-original-only and +7.7% over translated-only, with each track contributing unique evidence fields.

baseline_b.title: Multilingual Literature Coverage
baseline_b.question: Do non-English papers contain variant evidence that English-only retrieval misses?
baseline_b.dataset: 1,602 filtered papers across 7 languages (en/zh/ja/ko/es/pt/ru), filtered from 6,667 scanned
baseline_b.methodology: Compare gene and variant (HGVS + rsID) coverage between English-only and the full multilingual corpus

gene_coverage.interpretation: English covers most gene symbols well — non-English literature adds marginal gene-level coverage

variant_coverage.interpretation: 78.7% of specific variants (HGVS c./p. notation, rsIDs) are found ONLY in non-English papers. This represents population-specific variant evidence invisible to English-only retrieval.

baseline_b.conclusion: While English covers gene-level coverage well, 78.7% of specific variant evidence (HGVS + rsID) exists only in non-English literature. Korean and Chinese contribute the most unique variants.

key_findings: Non-English literature contains 363 variants (78.7% of total) not found in English papers — these represent population-specific evidence that English-only databases systematically miss
Dual-track extraction (original + translated) improves evidence extraction F1 by +5.5% over single-track, with each track contributing unique fields
Korean (86) and Chinese (81) non-English papers contribute the most unique variants, followed by Spanish (74) and Russian (57)
Genes are well-covered by English (93.5%), but the specific variants within those genes are overwhelmingly non-English (78.7%) — this is the core evidence gap
combined_interpretation.narrative: Existing English-centric databases cover the right genes but miss 78.7% of the specific variants within those genes. LinguaSeeker's multilingual retrieval captures these population-specific variants, while dual-track extraction ensures extraction quality from non-English text.
